title: The covenant service
hookLine: the Methodist covenant prayer: put me to doing, put me to suffering
tomorrow: a hymn says the whole world would be too small a gift. for what?

cards: Terms and conditions. Scroll, scroll, scroll, I agree. Nobody reads them; that's the joke.

A covenant is the opposite: you read every line, out loud, in front of people, and you mean it. In the Methodist covenant service, a congregation says a prayer with a line in it that stops people mid-breath.
Put me to doing, put me to suffering. So who would ever ask God to put them to suffering?

teach.b: Listen to how the prayer is built, and the puzzle undoes itself. It comes in pairs. Put me to doing, put me to suffering.
Employed for you, or laid aside for you. Exalted, or brought low. Let me be full, let me be empty.
Let me have all things, let me have nothing. Every pair has an easy half and a hard half. The prayer doesn't ask for the hard half.
It hands over the choosing. Whichever half comes, the answer is the same, and it arrives near the end: I am thine.

teach.h: BOTH TO BE FULL AND TO BE HUNGRY.
teach.b: It's Paul's attitude in his letter to the Philippians, put into the mouth of a whole congregation: "every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need."
Wesley drew the service from older Puritan writers and gave it to the Methodists, and Methodist churches still hold it, often near the new year. You can feel the pairs in your own two hands.

teach.h: A FULL HAND, AN EMPTY HAND.

teach.b: An empty hand opens. The prayer asks for neither one; it asks that both belong to God. One to tell a friend: the hardest-sounding line is half of a pair, and the other half is joy.

how: Many Methodist churches hold a covenant service, often on the first Sunday of the year, when the congregation says the covenant prayer together; some Christians of other churches pray it privately.

o: a Methodist service of handing yourself over to God, in pairs
a wedding service where vows are read in front of everyone
a church meeting where members sign a building contract

games.q: the prayer in pairs — tap the pairs.

s: the covenant prayer asks God to send hardship
every line is a pair, an easy half and a hard half. it hands over the choosing, not a request for pain.
Paul tells the Philippians he has learned both to be full and to be hungry
both to abound and to suffer need: the same pairs the prayer uses.
Wesley wrote the covenant service entirely on his own
he drew it from older Puritan writers and gave it to the Methodists.

games.q: your mom, a nurse, is offered a promotion: fewer patients, more meetings. she's torn and says she'll pray the covenant prayer. what does it hand over?
o: the choosing itself: employed or laid aside, either way 'I am thine'.
only the hard option: the prayer means pick whatever hurts most.
nothing yet: it's a prayer for the new year, not for decisions.
games.why: the pairs cover both roads. the prayer doesn't tell her which to take; it gives both to God.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees. Close one into a loose fist, full, and leave the other open, empty, palm up. Breathe in, and feel both; breathe out, and turn the fist slowly open to match the other.
If you pray, the covenant's short line can go with that last breath: I am thine.

wordCard.voice: The covenant service. A Methodist congregation hands over the easy half and the hard half together, and ends: I am thine.

carryVoice: Your line: I am thine. Full hand or empty one, the prayer's answer doesn't change. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: The Methodist covenant prayer (from Wesley's Directions for Renewing Our Covenant with God, after Joseph and Richard Alleine)
